A blazon is a precise, formal verbal description of a coat of arms — written in a strict, specialized language that tells you exactly what the coat of arms looks like, piece by piece, in a specific order.
What is a coat of arms, and why does it need a blazon?

To understand blazon, you first need a small amount of context.

In medieval Europe, knights, noble families, and institutions each had a unique visual symbol — a coat of arms — displayed on shields, banners, and official documents. It identified who they were, much like a logo identifies a company today.

The problem: if you only had the picture of a coat of arms, but no written record of it, and the original artist died, you might end up with slightly different versions of the same coat of arms over time — like a game of telephone played with paintings.

The solution was the blazon: a written description so precise and standardized that a trained herald (an official expert in coats of arms) could read it and recreate the exact coat of arms without ever having seen the original picture. The blazon is the authoritative record of a coat of arms, even more so than any painting of it.

A blazon is not just a casual description like "there's a red background with a golden lion on it." It is written in a highly specific, rule-governed language — essentially a formal grammar developed specifically for heraldry — that eliminates any ambiguity.

This language:

Uses its own vocabulary for colors. In a blazon, colors are never called "red" or "blue." Instead, they have official heraldic names: Gules (red), Azure (blue), Or (gold), Argent (silver), Sable (black), Vert (green), Purpure (purple). These terms are precise and universal among heralds.

Uses its own vocabulary for animals and objects. An animal's exact posture, position, and orientation is described using specific terms. A lion standing upright on its hind legs is rampant. A lion walking with one paw raised is passant. These terms are not interchangeable — each describes something visually distinct.

Follows a strict order. A blazon always describes things in a fixed sequence: first the background (called the field), then the most important central element (the charge), then lesser elements, and so on. This fixed order means the description is always predictable and readable.

A simple example of a blazon: "Gules, a lion rampant Or."
This means: a red background, with a golden lion rearing up on its hind legs. An expert reading just those four words could draw the coat of arms accurately.
The blazon as a living document

The blazon of a coat of arms was the official record kept in heraldic registries. When a family was granted a coat of arms, the blazon was what was formally recorded. It was the legal, definitive description. Disputes about what a coat of arms "really" looked like were settled by going back to the blazon.

Over the centuries, the same coat of arms might be painted in slightly different styles by different artists — the lion might look more muscular or more graceful depending on the era — but the blazon remained constant and authoritative.

Over time, the word "blazon" extended slightly beyond strict heraldry:

1. The coat of arms itself (not just its description).
Sometimes people use "blazon" to refer to the actual coat of arms — the visual emblem as a whole — not merely the written description of it. This is a slightly looser usage but commonly accepted. You might hear: "The blazon of the university was carved above the entrance." Here, blazon simply means the heraldic emblem.

2. A public display or conspicuous proclamation.
In more literary or formal writing, "blazon" can mean a public, prominent display or announcement of something — usually something honorable or notable. For example: "The blazon of her achievements was posted across the hall." This usage draws on the idea that coats of arms were boldly displayed in public as declarations of identity and honor.

• A blazon is not a picture; it is a description in words that tells you how to produce the picture. (Though by extension, it can also refer to the heraldic image itself.)
  • A blazon is not a general description of anything visual. It specifically belongs to the world of heraldry, and its extended meanings trace directly back to that origin.
  • It is not the same as the coat of arms in totality. Strictly speaking, the coat of arms is the visual design; the blazon is the written specification of that design.

A blazon is the precise, rule-governed written description of a coat of arms, using a specialized heraldic vocabulary and a fixed grammatical order, such that the image can be accurately reproduced from the words alone — and by extension, it can refer to the heraldic emblem itself, or any bold public display.
